@graph.headline: How Much to Risk Per Trade? Position Sizing Formula

acceptedAnswer.text: Position Size = (Account Equity × Risk%) ÷ (Entry Price − Stop-Loss Price). Multiply your account by the percentage you're willing to risk, divide by the per-share distance to your stop, and you get the quantity that loses exactly your risk budget if the stop is hit — see the worked example at the top of this article.

mainEntity.name: What is the position sizing formula?

acceptedAnswer.text: Risk no more than 1% of your total account equity on any single trade — on a ₹1,00,000 account, that's ₹1,000 maximum loss per trade. It exists because of the compounding math of losses: at 1% risk it takes 69 consecutive losses to halve an account, versus about 7 at 10% risk.

mainEntity.name: What is the 1% rule in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: 0.5% to 1% of account equity per trade. Start at 1% as the standard default, drop to 0.5% while learning a new strategy or running anything with long expected losing streaks — the full risk% decision table shows what each level survives.

mainEntity.name: How much should a beginner risk per trade?

acceptedAnswer.text: Fix your entry and stop from your setup, choose your risk% (1% default), multiply account equity by risk% for your rupee risk budget, divide by (entry − stop) for your quantity, and round DOWN. The classic edge case: a ₹3 stop on a ₹1,00,000 account at 1% risk gives 333 shares — a ₹3.43 lakh notional that exceeds the account, so the formula's honest answer is "you cannot afford this trade."

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate position size?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mathematically optimal for long-run growth, psychologically unusable at full strength: a 10-loss streak at 32.5% full Kelly leaves ~2% of your capital (~98% drawdown). Professionals use fractional Kelly — 1/4 to 1/2 of the full number — which keeps most of the growth with far tamer drawdowns; see Kelly is Expectancy, plugged in.

mainEntity.name: Is the Kelly Criterion good for traders?

acceptedAnswer.text: None is universally best: fixed fractional is the standard default — simple, auto-scales down in drawdowns; fixed dollar is simpler but doesn't scale; Kelly is the mathematical growth ceiling but demands verified inputs and fractional use. The comparison table lays out the trade-offs.

mainEntity.name: Fixed fractional vs fixed dollar vs Kelly — which is better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Then the formula has given you a legitimate answer: you cannot afford this trade. Three honest responses — skip it, accept the stop is too tight for your account size, or (intraday) use margin to carry the notional while keeping the rupee risk unchanged; never move the stop or round the size up to force it. See the ₹3 stop problem.

mainEntity.name: What if my calculated position size exceeds my capital?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Sizing controls variance and drawdown, not expectancy — multiplying a negative per-trade expectancy by any position size keeps it negative. It decides whether you survive long enough to collect your edge; only the edge itself decides whether you win. Full argument in the myth-bust section and our risk-of-ruin guide.

mainEntity.name: Can position sizing make a losing strategy profitable?

acceptedAnswer.text: 1% of your account per trade is the standard default — on ₹1,00,000 that is ₹1,000. Beginners should start at 0.5% to 1% while learning a new strategy.
